direction.premise: A cooperative falling-block arcade rebuilt around a legible single shared well, even on narrow phones.
direction.composition: An editorial start screen leads to a shared crisp falling-block well. On cooperative games a colored multi-gate gantry anchors each player exactly above their four-cell entrance, while touch controls sit at thumb reach. An automatically dark evening palette maintains low luminance on every setup and result screen; desktop forms use broad two-column structures. The four-cell inlets and two-cell previews now occupy a single contiguous grid plane aligned to the playable canvas with hairline colored rails carrying visually into the first two board rows. The post-match report uses a safe-area-aware scrollable shell with a reachable sticky replay action even in short landscape viewports.
direction.shapeLanguage: Crisp square stack cells, quiet linear menu rows, pill-free directional keys and one heavy color-filled hard-drop key. The top gate is one contiguous industrial inlet instead of floating separate preview boxes. Personal identity is encoded with thin vertical lane lips and faint board-entry traces rather than boxed preview cards; eliminated gates shut with a restrained diagonal hatch.
direction.surfaceAndMaterial: Warm paper shell and sage hardware borders surround a dark deep-green playing well; no glass overlays, purple gradients or neon chromed cabinet.
direction.paletteLogic: A neutral matte shell yields attention to player-owned cyan, pink, yellow and green cells; the hard-drop key is deep green.
direction.typography: Humanist sans for mode choices, tightly-spaced monospace for score and technical status; labels stay concise.
direction.signature: Four-cell by two-cell colored individual spawn gates extend directly above the shared well; every gate has the player name and own next-piece indicator. Input and gameplay remain one instrument.
direction.distinction: Distinct from ZAMAZKA's art paper and FOG's tactical maps: this is a fitted precision arcade well within a restrained editorial instrument, not a decorative game cabinet.
direction.motion: A bounded canvas overlay adds brief stamped block impact, row fracture and clear-combo rising score, independent of game logic and keyboard/touch flow; prefers-reduced-motion removes these effects. Procedural low-frequency impact and tonal crystalline clears replace shrill flat beeps, while the existing mute toggle remains functional.
direction.interaction: Connected teammates automatically inherit host permissions after host socket loss, while a compact in-game recovery bar offers one explicit reconnect action without forcing the user into a new menu. Settings navigation suspends local physics without changing the board and resumes its clock on return; key capture has an explicit Escape cancellation. A live server round cannot be replaced by a decorative debug preview.

architecture.primaryVerb: Place falling pieces into the one shared well: hold horizontal movement or soft-drop, rotate with a tap, swipe in whole-cell steps, or hard-drop.
architecture.physicalFeedback: Two-thumb buttons depress by 3px on pointer contact, local gestures resolve immediately, online snapshots reconcile to the authoritative well.
architecture.spatialRationale: Keep 20-row board cell precision at all breakpoints; dedicate four columns and two rows of visible gate to each player. Place next-piece preview and player nickname immediately over their individual gate, rather than a disjoint sidebar. The four gates remain aligned under aspect-ratio changes.

comparisons.interactionDifference: Blockies requires cell-precise hold, canvas swipe and fast hard drop, with PocketNet authoritative shared state instead of perekos interaction.

comparisons.spatialDifference: Black Bazaar emphasizes collections and marketplace information panels; Blockies retains one unbroken, center-weighted 20-row play well, a slim score rail, and a thumb-reachable control deck.
comparisons.interactionDifference: Trade decisions and inventory inspection do not translate into the one-cell, continuous gravity-based movement, rotation and instant hard drop required by Blockies.

comparisons.spatialDifference: Picto arranges communal symbol and clue slots for group interpretation, while Blockies gives the falling board priority and moves its reward register into an optional overlay away from active play.
comparisons.interactionDifference: Picto's deliberate simultaneous symbol choices differ from Blockies' real-time movement with repeat-on-hold controls and server-verified collaborative line clears.

comparisons.spatialDifference: Bozhe Ne Tak dedicates its split workspace to a carved god altar, tribute shelf and ritual props; Blockies keeps an uninterrupted pixel-accurate falling-block well and a narrow score rail with controls below.
comparisons.interactionDifference: Bozhe Ne Tak resolves discrete ritual offerings and deity judgments; Blockies is continuous real-time co-op, with repeat-on-hold motion and PocketNet snapshots synchronized for every falling piece.

comparisons.spatialDifference: Axis Pals uses a partnership puzzle workspace built around coordinating choices, while Blockies gives its one uninterrupted falling-block well a cell-aligned gantry of individual next-piece and spawn entrances.
comparisons.interactionDifference: The discrete joint decisions of Axis Pals differ from Blockies' repeat-on-hold movement and hard-drop physics, with independently blocked player entrances and server-authoritative board synchronization.

comparisons.spatialDifference: Crown Laws is a medieval council interface with document-like law choices and political consequences. Blockies instead keeps a narrow central pixel-grid arcade board and a coherent four-cell spawn gantry; large setup columns are for configuring physical controls, not storytelling.
comparisons.interactionDifference: Council decisions in Crown Laws advance political turns, whereas Blockies uses simultaneous real-time tetromino actions, live PocketNet snapshots, player-specific entry points and a compact data-backed post-round field recap.

comparisons.spatialDifference: Jam Tape is a collaborative instrument workstation arranged around tracks, playback and tape controls. Blockies remains a shared uninterrupted cell grid with an exact-width top gantry physically aligned to individual tetromino entrances.
comparisons.interactionDifference: Recording and mixing on a timeline in Jam Tape differs from Blockies' simultaneous gravity-driven piece navigation, split-lane spawn gates and deterministic server collision checks.

comparisons.spatialDifference: Ne Zhmi is built around the user deciding whether to press a tempting control; Blockies centers a long shared playfield with narrow segmented but unboxed preview bays that are visually part of the board.
comparisons.interactionDifference: Ne Zhmi's discrete one-off button choice is unlike continuous falling-block movement, rotation, hard dropping, player-specific blocked-entry elimination and high-frequency authoritative snapshots.

comparisons.spatialDifference: Moss & Marble frames a mini-golf course as a navigable sculpted outdoor landscape with depth, course walls and a ball trajectory; Blockies concentrates on a fixed shared vertical well with four-cell entry gantries and compact network recovery controls.
comparisons.interactionDifference: Golf swings and course geometry are turn-by-turn physics challenges, while Blockies uses simultaneous keyboard/touch falling-block movement, deterministic locking and server-authoritative recovery of entire co-op rounds.

production.renderer: Canvas 2D paints crisp, flat tiles with light rims and ghost landings; source collision, scoring, seeded pieces and server-authoritative online rules are preserved.
production.focalAsset: A dark shared well with personal 4×2 colored inlet gates, a clipped next-tetromino preview and a label for every teammate; one coherent geometric stack-shaped icon.

motion.character: Gravity, directional repeat and swipe displacement use visible cell-by-cell changes, never interpolation that misrepresents landing coordinates.
motion.action: Move and rotate your own falling piece, then drop it into the shared stack while leaving room for the other player.
motion.anticipation: Each player's named colored 4×2 bay previews their next piece directly above the exact spawn entrance. An obstructed entrance visibly closes for that player alone.
motion.response: A key depresses on touch, then the piece moves or rotates; hard drop snaps to the ghost position; server snapshots remain authoritative.
motion.followThrough: A filled personal entrance stops only its own player's pieces, with a visible blocked gate; the remaining teammates keep clearing the shared field. A scored match finishes with actual board-cell occupancy, teammate states and a final miniature stack, not decorative statistics.
motion.interruption: Pointer cancel, disconnect and app background release held controls; room rejoin restores authoritative state.
motion.reducedMotion: Prefer-reduced-motion strips UI transitions without affecting Tetris gravity or button/input semantics.

evidence.expectedChange: Mode selection opens the 20-row shared board with crisp cells, a next-piece rail and independent direction/rotation/hard-drop controls fitted to the viewport.
